Neonatal Chinese alligators (Alligator sinensis) emerge from parchment-shelled eggs after an incubation period that is strongly temperature-dependent. When eggs are incubated at a constant 25.5 °C [T = 25.5 °C], the age at birth is approximately 70 days [ab = approximately 70 days], a duration that aligns with the lower thermal limit for successful development in this species. Hatchlings typically measure about 21 centimeters [Lb = about 21 centimeters] in total length from snout to tail tip, and they carry a modest wet weight at birth of roughly 30 grams [Wwb = roughly 30 grams]. This neonate mass is supported by residual yolk reserves that sustain the young reptile through the first few weeks of life until the onset of exogenous feeding. The initial wet weight of the freshly laid, fertilized egg, prior to any significant embryonic development, has been recorded at 45 grams [Ww0 = 45 grams], indicating a substantial investment of maternal resources into each offspring given the species’ relatively small adult body size compared to its larger American cousin.

Sexual maturation in Alligator sinensis proceeds gradually, with individuals reaching puberty at a total length of approximately 101 centimeters [Lp = approximately 101 centimeters]. This length at sexual maturity was estimated by applying the relative scaling relationship observed in the closely related and better-studied Alligator mississippiensis, where puberty occurs at roughly 180 centimeters in a species that attains an ultimate female length of about 304 centimeters. Under captive conditions maintained at a stable 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the time since birth at puberty for female Chinese alligators is approximately 6 years [tp = approximately 6 years], though this interval can vary between 5 and 7 years depending on individual growth rates and food availability. Reproductive maturity is accompanied by a marked deceleration in somatic growth as resources are increasingly diverted toward gametogenesis and nesting behavior. The onset of gonadal activation marks a critical life-history transition for these long-lived reptiles.

Adult body size in Chinese alligators exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, a common pattern among crocodilians. Females attain an ultimate total length of 170 centimeters [Li = 170 centimeters], whereas males grow considerably larger, reaching an ultimate total length of 210 centimeters [Li = 210 centimeters]. This difference in linear dimensions translates into a substantial disparity in body mass. The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown female is approximately 23,900 grams [Wwi = approximately 23,900 grams], while a large male can achieve an ultimate wet weight of about 45,000 grams [Wwi = about 45,000 grams], nearly double that of the female. This size advantage likely confers benefits in male-male competition for access to nesting females and in the defense of breeding territories. The pronounced sexual size dimorphism influences not only social dynamics but also the energetic requirements and foraging ecology of each sex throughout the year.

Reproductive output in the Chinese alligator is constrained by the female's body size and the thermal conditions of the nesting environment. Under a thermal regime of 23 °C [T = 23 °C], females produce between 10 and 40 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 10 and 40 eggs per clutch], and typically a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year]. This annual reproductive effort represents a considerable energetic investment, as a large clutch may constitute a significant fraction of the female's body mass. The timing of nesting is closely tied to the summer monsoon season in the species' native range of the lower Yangtze River basin, where warm, humid conditions prevail. Nest site selection is critical, as the incubation temperature of the mound nest determines both the sex ratio of the hatchlings and the duration of embryonic development. Predation of nests by wild boar and other scavengers can be a major source of egg mortality in natural populations.

Longevity data for Alligator sinensis, gathered from both captive colonies and field recapture studies, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 65 years [am = approximately 65 years] when individuals are maintained at a consistent temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This extended lifespan is characteristic of large-bodied ectotherms with slow metabolic rates and low annual reproductive investment. The species exhibits indeterminate growth, though the rate of increase in total length slows considerably after sexual maturity is achieved. Maximum recorded adult body sizes in the wild generally approach the upper limits observed in captivity, suggesting that the asymptotic lengths reported are biologically realistic estimates of the species' growth potential. Conservation efforts for this critically endangered crocodilian hinge on understanding its slow life-history pace, as populations are slow to recover from declines caused by habitat loss and historical overharvesting.
